prompt: Pixel art in the style of a 1984 Commodore 64 game title screen, 16-colour palette, crisp square pixels with no anti-aliasing. Two friends sit at opposite ends of the El Segundo beach boardwalk at dusk, each holding a phone. Between the phones, a dotted line of glowing square packets arcs over the sand, each packet a different colour: calm blue, hyped red, soft purple, sunny yellow, salty green, tired grey-violet, curious orange, low indigo. Refinery lights and the pier on the horizon, deep C64 blue sky with a few stars. A thick light-purple screen border frames the scene. No words, no logos.

A warm, slightly grainy photograph of a beige 1980s home-computer monitor on a wooden desk by a window with late afternoon California light. The curved CRT shows a classic blue boot screen in a chunky 8-bit font reading exactly: READY. and below it LOAD "FRIEND",8,1 with a blinking block cursor. A modern smartphone lies on the desk next to the keyboard, its screen glowing the same blue. Shallow depth of field, no brand names or logos anywhere.

Isometric pixel art, Atari 800 era palette, crisp pixels. One hand holds a phone showing a large black-and-white QR code; a second phone in another hand points its camera at it, with a yellow square scanning frame on its screen. A thin line of coloured square packets jumps from one phone to the other. Deep blue background with a subtle scanline texture. No words, no logos.

Pixel art diagram brought to life, Commodore 64 palette: five chunky pixel phones arranged in a pentagon on a deep blue field, every phone linked to every other by glowing dotted lines, ten links in all. One phone has a small yellow crown above it (the host). Each phone's screen shows a different mood colour. Clean, readable, no words, no logos.

Pixel art still life, 16-colour palette: a paper bar tab with handwritten pixel scribbles pinned under a coffee cup on a beach-cafe table, and a single glowing blue coin with a stylised lowercase t-like symbol hovering above it, with a small green check mark. Late-afternoon light, deep shadows in dithered pixels. No readable words, no real logos.

Pixel art cutaway of a tiny cosy control room at night, Commodore 64 palette: eight small friendly box-shaped robots each at their own glowing terminal, each terminal a different colour, wires running from every terminal to a central desk where one robot with a clipboard checks items off a list. A window shows the El Segundo pier at night. Charming, busy, no words, no logos.

Pixel art split sky, left half a calm blue morning over the Pacific, right half a warm orange evening over a far-away city, the two skies blending in the middle through dithered bands. A small chat bubble floats in each half, connected by a thin line of square packets. Atari 800 palette, crisp pixels, no words, no logos.

A 1982 home-video-game box art poster, painted illustration style with bold diagonal rainbow stripes (red, orange, yellow, green, blue) across a black top band. The painting shows two teenagers on opposite rooftops at night trading glowing messages that travel as coloured squares across the sky over a Southern California beach town. At the top, large chunky retro lettering reads PMM. Small text at the bottom reads POINTCAST MOBILE MESSAGING. No other text and no real brand logos.
